CLUSTERS UNDER SFURTI SCHEME IN RAJASTHAN 
 
*170.    SHRI HARISH CHANDRA MEENA:  
 
Will the Minister of MICRO, SMALL AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES be pleased to state:  
 
(a)  the number of clusters approved, ongoing and completed under the Scheme of Fund for 
Regeneration of Traditional Industries (SFURTI) in Rajasthan, district -wise including T onk and 
Sawai Madhopur;  
 
(b)  the total amount of funds sanctioned and utilized under the said scheme in Rajasthan since its 
inception, along with the number of artisans and traditional workers directly benefited therefrom, 
gender- wise; 
 
(c)  whether the Government has identified traditional industry clusters such as stone carving, 
carpet weaving and handloom in the Tonk -Sawai Madhopur, Lok Sabha Constituency for support 
under the said scheme or Micro and Small Enterprises-Cluster Development Programme (MSE-CDP) 
and if so, the details thereof; 
 
(d)  the monitoring mechanism in place to assess the income growth of artisans after the 
completion of SFURTI clusters; and 
 
(e)  the corrective steps taken to address the gaps/shortfall in achieving the targets for  income 
growth of artisans, if any? 
 
ANSWER 
 
MINISTER OF MICRO, SMALL AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES 
(SHRI JITAN RAM MANJHI) 
 
(a) to (e):  A Statement laid on the Table of the House. 
 
  

 
 
 
 
STATEMENT REFERRED TO IN REPLY TO THE PARTS OF (a) to (e) OF LOK SABHA 
STARRED QUESTION NO. *170 FOR ANSWER ON 30.07.2026. 
 
(a): Under the Scheme of Fund for Regeneration of Traditional Industries (SFURTI), which was 
in operation upto  September, 2022, 34 clusters have been approved in Rajasthan. Out of these, 25 
clusters are functional and 09 clusters are in progress. The district -wise (including Tonk and Sawai 
Madhopur) number of approved, functional and in -progress clusters in Rajast han are placed at 
Annexure-I. 
 
(b): The total committed Government of India (GoI) assistance for 34 approved clusters in 
Rajasthan is Rs. 93.00 crore, out of which Rs. 78.95 crore has been released and utilized. These 
clusters are benefiting 18,209 artisans, comprising 9,715 male artisans and 8,494 female artisans.  
 
(c): Under the SFURTI Scheme, three clusters have been approved in the Tonk-Sawai Madhopur 
Lok Sabha Constituency, for carpet weaving, handicrafts and beekeeping/honey processing. 
However, no proposal related to stone carving and handloom cluster has been received under the 
Micro and Small Enterprises Cluster Development Programme (MSE -CDP)for the Tonk–Sawai 
Madhopur Lok Sabha Constituency. 
 
(d): As per the Scheme Guidelines, the performance and sustainability of SFURTI clusters, 
including indicators relating to artisans' livelihoods and income generation, are monitored through a 
multi-tier mechanism inv olving the Implementing Agency (IA), Technical Agency (TA), Nodal 
Agency (NA) and the Ministry. The monitoring mechanism includes periodic review meetings, field 
visits, monitoring of production and sales, utilisation of Common Facility Centres (CFCs), mar ket 
linkages, and audited reports, along with review of cluster-level data relating to production, sales and 
other operational parameters to assess cluster performance and sustainability. 
 
(e): Wherever gaps or shortfalls are identified, corrective measures are  undertaken through 
strengthened monitoring, capacity -building and visits, improved utilisation of CFCs, enhanced 
market linkages through participation in fairs, exhibitions and technical handholding, wherever 
feasible, to improve artisans' income-generating opportunities and ensure long-term sustainability of 
the clusters.

MINISTRY OF POWER 
 
LOK SABHA 
STARRED QUESTION NO.171 
ANSWERED ON 30.07.2026 
 
IMPACT OF RISING ELECTRICITY DEMAND IN PUNJAB 
 
*171. DR. AMAR SINGH: 
 
Will the Minister of POWER 
be pleased to state: 
 
(a) whether the Government has assessed the impact of the rising electricity 
demand in Punjab on the State's long-term energy security, particularly during 
the paddy transplantation season and if so, the details thereof;  
 
(b) the assistance provided for strengthening transmission and distributi on 
infrastructure, improving grid reliability and integrating renewable energy 
under various Government programmes;  
 
(c) whether any policy has been formulated to promote solarisation of 
agricultural pump sets, energy -efficient irrigation systems and dema nd-side 
management to reduce agricultural power consumption and if so, the details 
thereof;  
 
(d) whether any mechanism is in place to ensure reliable electricity supply 
during peak agricultural seasons while maintaining the financial sustainability 
of distribution utilities and if so, the details thereof; and  
 
(e) the measures proposed to strengthen long -term power security, improve 
energy efficiency and reduce dependence on costly external power 
procurement? 
A N S W E R 
 
THE MINISTER OF POWER  
 
(SHRI MANOHAR LAL)  
 
(a) to (e) : A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
 
******* 
  

 
STATEMENT 
 
STATEMENT REFERRED TO IN REPLY TO PARTS (a) TO (e) IN RESPECT OF LOK 
SABHA STARRED QUESTION NO. 171 FOR REPLY ON 30.07.2026 REGARDING 
IMPACT OF RISING ELECTRICIT Y DEMAND IN PUNJAB  ASKED BY DR. AMAR 
SINGH 
*********** 
(a) :  The Central Electricity Authority (CEA) assesses the country's electricity 
requirement and peak demand on a year-on-year basis at the national, regional, 
State, and Union Territory (UT) levels.  The details of month -wise energy 
requirement and peak demand of the State of Punjab for the period April to 
September during the last five years and current year (upto June, 2026) is given 
at Annexure-I. The electricity demand of Punjab increases during p addy 
transplantation season of June to September months every year. 
 
Further, with a view to ensure generation capacity remains ahead of 
projected peak demand, all the States including Punjab, in consultation with 
CEA, have prepared their “Resource Adequac y Plans (RAPs)”, which are 
dynamic 10-year rolling plans and includes power generation as well as power 
procurement planning. Accordingly, assessed energy requirement and peak 
demand of the Punjab from FY 2026-27 to 2031-32 is given at Annexure-II. 
 
(b) :  Government of India has taken the following measures for strengthening 
the transmission and distribution infrastructure, improving grid reliability & 
integrating renewable energy in the country including the state of Punjab: 
 
(i) Capacity addition from non-fossil Sources: Thrust is on capacity addition 
from non-fossil sources, which now exceeds 54% of the total installed 
electricity generation capacity. Further, Government has planned to 
achieve 500 GW of non-fossil fuel based installed generation capacity by 
2030. As per the National Generation Adequacy Plan prepared by CEA in 
March 2026, the non -fossil fuel based installed capacity is likely to 
increase to 786 GW by 2035-36.   
 
(ii) Capacity addition from Conventional Sources: It is projected to increase 
the insta lled capacity of coal -based plants to 315 GW by 2035 -36. 
Keeping in view energy security, no new imported coal -based power 
plants have been planned. 
 
(iii)  Nuclear power has huge potential to ensure long term energy security 
and is vital for India’s clean energy transition towards Net Zero by 2070. 
It is a clean and environment friendly source of base load power. The 
lifecycle emissions of nuclear power are comparable to those of 
renewables like hydro and wind.  Government of India has set an 
ambitious target of 100 GW nuclear power capacity by 2047. 
 
 

(iv)  Energy Storage Systems are being encouraged. Roadmap to 100 GW of 
Hydro Pumped Storage Projects by 2035 -36 has been prepared. As per 
the National Generation Adequacy Plan prepared by CEA in March 2026, 
the likely BESS installed capacity and PSP installed capacity in 2035-36 
is 80 GW and 94 GW respectively. 
 
(v) 100% Inter State Transmission System (ISTS) charges have been waived 
for inter -state sale of solar and wind power for projects to be 
commissioned by 30th June 2025 (with waiver tapering off 25% annually 
till June 2028), for co-located BESS projects commissioned by June 2028, 
for Hydro PSP projects where construction work awarded by June 2028, 
for Green Hydrogen Projects commissioned till December 2030 and for 
offshore wind projects commissioned till December 2032. 
 
(vi) Standard Bidding Guidelines for tariff based competitive bidding process 
for procurement of Power from Grid Connected Solar, Wind, Wind -Solar 
Hybrid and Firm & Dispatchable RE (FDRE) projects have been issued. 
 
(vii) Significant expansion of the transmission network has been undertaken 
since 2014, resulting in the addition of 2,18,267 circuit kilometres (ckm) 
of transmission lines, 9,47,405 MVA of transformation capacity and 
84,390 MW of inter -regional transmi ssion capacity. Consequently, the 
total inter-regional transmission capacity has reached 1,20,340 MW as 
on 30.06.2026, enabling reliable power transfer across the country. 
 
(viii) Government of India has been supplementing the efforts of States/ UTs 
to help them provide quality supply of power through schemes like Deen 
Dayal Upadhyaya Gram Jyoti Yojana (DDUGJY), Integrated Power 
Development Scheme (IPDS), Pradhan Mantri Sahaj Bijli Har Ghar Yojana 
(SAUBHAGYA). Under these schemes, projects worth Rs. 1.85 lakh Cr. 
were executed for strengthening of power distribution infrastructure. 
These schemes stand closed as on 31.03.2022. A total of 18,374 villages 
were electrified under DDUGJY and a total 2.86 crore households during 
SAUBHAGYA. During SAUBHAGYA, 3,477 house ho ld of Punjab were 
electrified. Presently under the Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme 
(RDSS), launched by Government of India in July 2021 with the objective 
of making distribution utilities operationally efficient and financially 
viable, financial assistance is being provided to distribution utilities for 
upgradation of distribution infrastructure & smart metering works, Under 
the scheme, projects worth Rs. 1.53 lakh crore for loss reduction 
infrastructure and Rs. 1.31 lakh crore for smart metering works have 
been sanctioned across the country. This includes loss reduction works 
amounting to Rs. 3,873 crore and smart metering works amounting to Rs. 
5,769 crore sanctioned for the State of Punjab. 
 
(ix) Laying of new transmission lines and creating new sub -station capacity 
has been funded under the Green Energy Corridor Scheme for evacuation 
of renewable power. In order to augment transmission infrastructure 
needed for steep RE trajectory, transmission plan has been prepared till 
2032. 
 

(x) Development of intra -state transmission network is being planned to 
keep pace with RE capacity addition. Strong inter connection of Inter -
State Transmission System (ISTS) RE schemes with the intra -state 
network to ensure better reliability in terms of anchoring voltage 
stability, angular stability, losses reduction etc. is being done.  
 
(xi) The Ministry of Heavy Industries has launched the PLI scheme namely 
“National Programme on Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC) Battery 
Storage,” approved in May 2021 with a total outlay of ₹18,100 crore to 
establish 50 GWh of domestic Advanced Chemistry Cell manufacturing 
capacity, out of which 10 GWh is earmarked for Grid Scale Stationary 
Storage (GSSS) applications. 
 
(xii) MoP in March, 2022 notified the Guidelines for Procurement and 
Utilization of Battery Ener gy Storage Systems as part of Generation, 
Transmission and Distribution assets, along with Ancillary Services. 
 
(xiii) MoP has notified Guidelines to promote development of Pumped Storage 
Projects in the country on 10th April, 2023. 
 
(xiv) Government of India, in Septe mber 2023, approved a Viability Gap 
Funding (VGF) scheme for development of Battery Energy Storage 
Systems (BESS). BESS capacity of 13.22 GWh is under implementation 
with a budgetary allocation of Rs 3,760 Cr. under this scheme. 
Considering the increasing demand of BESS, Ministry of Power, in June 
2025, has approved another VGF scheme for development of 30 GWh 
BESS capacity with financial support of Rs 5,400 Cr from Power System 
Development Fund (PSDF) including 500 MWh for Punjab with financial 
support of 90 Cr. 
 
(xv) Tariff Based Competitive Bidding (TBCB) guidelines have been issued for 
procurement of power from Pumped Storage Projects. 
 
(xvi) Central Electricity Authority (CEA) issued an advisory on 18.02.2025 
recommending the co -location of Energy Storage Systems (ESS) with 
solar power projects to enhance grid stability and cost efficiency. 
 
(xvii) CEA (Measures Relating to Safety and Electric Supply) (First Amendment) 
Regulations, 2025 has been notified on 30.03.2026, which includes the 
safety requirements for BESS. 
 
(c) & (d): The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy launched the Pradhan 
Mantri Kisan Urja Suraksha evam Utthaan Mahabhiyan (PM-KUSUM) scheme on 
8th March 2019 with the objective of promoting the solarisation of agricultural 
pump sets, including standalone sola r pumps. Under Component -C of the 
scheme, solarisation of 35 lakh existing grid -connected agricultural pumps is 
supported, including Feeder Level Solarization (FLS), along with the promotion 
of energy-efficient irrigation systems. The scheme is being implemented across 
all States and Union Territories, including Punjab. 

 
 
 
In Punjab, 186 Individual Pump Solarisation (IPS) systems have been 
sanctioned, and 17,928 off-grid solar pumps have been installed under the PM-
KUSUM scheme. 
   
Further, Government of India has been laying emphasis on segregation of 
mixed load feeders having more than 30% agricultural load, with the objective 
of efficient load management and enabling solarisation of agriculture feeders. 
In the State of Punjab, out of 6,932 feeders feasible for segregation, 6,705 
feeders have already been segregated under earlier schemes of the Central and 
State Governments. Under the ongoing RDSS, feeder segregation works 
amounting to Rs. 39,795 crores have been sanctioned for 31,109 feasible 
feeders across the country, including 227 feeders in Punjab with a sanctioned 
cost of Rs. 383 crores.  
 
In addition to RDSS, Government of India has taken the following measures 
for improving and maintaining the financial sustainability of DISCOMs: 
 
(i) Additional Borrowing space of 0.5% of Gross State Domestic Product 
(GSDP) to State Governments, which is conditional on them undertaking 
specific reforms in the power sector. 
 
(ii) Additional Prudential Norms for sanctioning of loans to State owned Power 
Utilities which would be co ntingent to the performance of Power 
Distribution Utilities against prescribed conditions. 
 
(iii) Rules for implementation of Fuel and Power Purchase Cost Adjustment 
(FPPCA) and Cost reflective tariff so as to ensure that all prudent cost for 
supply of electricity are passed through. 
 
(iv) Rules and Standard Operating Procedure issued for proper Subsidy 
Accounting and their timely payment. 
 
(v) Advisory to SERCs (State Electricity Regulatory Commission) & JERCs 
(Joint Electricity Regulatory Commission) for timely issuance of tariff and 
true up orders. 
 
 To ensure the reliable supply during peak agriculture season, Punjab 
state also uses seasonal variability of demand by entering into Banking/ 
swapping arrangement with other utilities having complimentary demand 
profile. 
  

 
 
(e):  As per Section 7 of Electricity Act, 2003 setting up of a power plant is a 
de-licensed activity in the country. Any generating company may establish, 
operate and maintain a generating station without requiring a license under 
Electricity Act, 2003 if it complies with the technical standards relating to 
connectivity with the grid. 
  
 
As per the Resource Adequacy (RA) study, the total projected 
contracted capacity requirement for Punjab for the year 2035 –36 is estimated 
at approximately 42,263 MW. This includes 12,043 MW from coal, 137 MW from 
gas, 197 MW from nuclear, 234 MW from biomass, 3,684 MW from hydro, 4,950 
MW from wind, 16,807 MW from solar, and 3,211 MW from Distributed 
Renewable Energy (DRE) sources, along with 2,812 MW / 13,082 MWh of energy 
storage capacity. In addition, around 8,000 MW of power procurement through 
Medium-Term Open Access (MTOA) and Short -Term Open Access (STOA) is 
projected to be required to reliably meet the demand. 
 
 As on 30.06.2026, a total of 13,808 MW operational capa city is 
available with Punjab State. This comprises of 3,829 MW from the state sector, 
6,989 MW from the private sector, and 2,991 MW allocated from Central 
Generating Stations (CGS). Further, Power Purchase Agreement (PPAS) / Power 
Supply Agreements (PSAs ) of 2,960 MW of renewable energy capacity is 
executed by Punjab State Power Corporation Ltd. (PSPCL).

MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION 
LOK SABHA

 ( TO BE ANSWERED ON THE  30th July 2026 )  
AWARENESS REGARDING PASSENGER RIGHTS  
172.    SHRI SURESH KUMAR SHETKAR                
Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION 
be pleased to state:- 
(a) whether the Government has assessed that awareness among passengers regarding their 
civil aviation rights remains low and if so, the details thereof along with the steps taken to 
conduct nationwide awareness campaigns and improve transparency; 
 
(b) whether the digital platforms for filing passenger complaints are user -friendly and 
effective and if so, the details thereof including the statistics on their usage, complaint 
resolution rates and the improvements proposed; 
 
(c) whether the  Government proposes to introduce stricter penalties including suspension of 
licences for repeated violations by airlines and if so, the details thereof including the Policy 
changes under consideration; 
 
(d) whether the recent surge in air traffic has adve rsely affected service quality and 
compliance with passenger rights and if so, the details thereof along with the measures taken 
to ensure that airlines maintain the prescribed standards; and 
 
(e) whether the Government proposes to amend the existing aviation regulations to strengthen 
passenger protections, if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
ANSWER 
Minister of CIVIL AVIATION      (Shri Kinjarapu Rammohan Naidu) 
(a) to (e): A statement is laid on the table of the house. 
****** 
  

STATEMENT REFERRED TO IN REPLY TO PARTS (A) TO (E) IN 
RESPECT OF LOK SABHA STARRED QUESTION NO. 172 FOR REPLY 
ON 30.07.2026 REGARDING "AWARENESS REGARDING PASSENGER 
RIGHTS" BY SHRI SURESH KUMAR SHETKAR 
 
(a): Ministry of Civil Aviation (MoCA) has issued the P assenger Charter to 
ensure that air travellers are aware of their rights and responsibilities. The 
Charter outlines passengers' rights in situations such as flight delays, flight 
cancellations, denied boarding due to overbooking, ticket refunds, flight 
diversions, medical emergencies and lost, delayed or damaged baggage.  
 
To enhance passenger awareness, all airports are required to display a QR code 
linking to the Passenger Charter under the heading "Know Your Rights When 
You Fly" at check -in counters, boa rding gates and other prominent locations 
within airport terminals. In addition, all airlines have been instructed to share 
the link to the Passenger Charter at the time of ticket booking through digital 
messages or by displaying it on the ticket itself. 
 
(b): The AirSewa portal, an initiative by MoCA, enables grievance redressal in 
a time-bound manner and provides a one -stop solution for hassle-free air travel. 
It allows passengers to submit and track grievances related to various 
stakeholders such as Ai rlines, Airports, Security, DGCA, Customs, 
Immigration, BCAS under various grievance categories including Baggage 
Claim. 
 
Further, the Ministry has established a permanent, 24*7 Passenger Assistance 
Control Room (PACR) to enhance passenger-centric governance. This initiative 
integrates MoCA, DGCA, AAI and airlines for real -time monitoring of flight 
disruptions, baggage issues and refunds, aiming to accelerate grievance 
redressal and improve the overall travel experience. 
 
The total grievances received d uring the period from 01.01.2026 to 30.06.2026 
were 64,641, of which 64,546 have been resolved, resulting in resolution rate of 
99.85%. 
 
(c): Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) has issued various passenger 
centric Civil Aviation Requirements (C ARs), to ensure adequate protection for 
air travellers and safeguard the interests of the travelling public. To monitor 
compliance with the provisions of the relevant CAR by the airline, DGCA 

conducts surveillance inspections and spot checks at airports across the country. 
In case of non -compliance, enforcement action, including imposition of 
financial penalty, is taken by DGCA. 
 
(d): Passenger traffic at airports vary depending on several factors such as 
seasonal demand, festivals, holidays, and airline schedules. During peak travel 
periods, higher passenger footfall may be observed at some airports which could 
lead to temporary congestion. However, airport operators continuously monitor 
passenger traffic and take necessary operational measures to ensure smooth 
passenger facilitation and efficient airport operations. 
 
(e): In order to ensure appropriate protection for the air travellers, DGCA has 
issued following passenger centric regulations/circulars to safeguard the interest 
of the travelling public: 
(i) Carriage by Air of Persons with Disability and/ or Persons with Reduced 
Mobility (CAR Section 3, Series M, Part I). 
(ii) Facilities to be provided to passengers by airlines due to denied boarding, 
cancellation of flights and delays in flights (CAR Section 3, Series M, Part IV). 
(iii) Refund of Airline Tickets to Passengers (CAR Section 3, Series M, Part II).  
 
The above CARs are revised from time to time to enhance passenger protection.

HOUSES UNDER PMAY - U 2.0 IN DUMKA, JHARKHAND 
 
 
NO. 173 SHRI NALIN SOREN:  
 
Will the Minister of HOUSING AND URBAN AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
 
(a) whether the Government has sanctioned houses under Pradhan 
Mantri Awas Yojana - Urban 2.0 (PMAY-U 2.0) in Dumka Municipal 
Council area of Jharkhand; 
(b) if so, the number of houses sanctioned,  under construction and 
completed so far under the said yojana; 
(c) the amount of central assistance sanctioned and released so far 
to Dumka Municipal Council under the said yojana; and 
(d) whether the Government proposes to take any special steps to 
provide housing to eligible beneficiaries at the earliest and settle 
the pending cases in a time- bound manner in Dumka Municipal 
Council and if so, the details thereof? 
 
ANSWER 
THE MINISTER OF HOUSING AND URBAN AFFAIRS 
(SHRI MANOHAR LAL) 
 
(a) to (d): A statement is laid on the Table of the House.  
 
 
 
 
 
 

STATEMENT REFERRED TO IN THE LOK SABHA STARRED QUESTION NO. 
173* ( 13TH POSITION) DUE FOR ANSWER ON 30.07.2026 REGARDING 
“HOUSES UNDER PMAY-U 2.0 IN DUMKA, JHARKHAND” 
 
(a) to (c):    Based on the project proposals received from the State 
Government of Jharkhand, a total of 14,187 houses have been sanctioned 
with the Central Assistance of ₹ 211.57 crore under Pradhan Mantri Awas 
Yojana – Urban 2.0 (PMAY-U 2.0). Out of this, a meagre figure of 118 houses 
are sanctioned in Dumka Municipal Council with the approved Central 
Assistance of ₹1.76 crore. The first instalment of 40% of approved Central 
Assistance against the approved houses in Dumka Municipal Council, i.e. 
₹70.2 lakh will be given to state government through mother sanction under 
SNA-SPARSH within a month. The progress of the scheme can also be 
accessed on the PMAY -U dashboard ( https://dashboard.pmay-urban.gov.in). 
 
 
(d):  PMAY-U 2.0 adopts a demand driven approach and no target has been 
fixed by the Government. States/ Union Territories ( UTs) assess the 
requirement through their Urban Local Bodies (ULBs)/Implementing Agencies 
in their respective jurisdictions. Eligible citizens apply through Unified Web 
Portal of PMAY-U 2.0 with all details on the portal. States/UTs/ULBs validate 
the beneficiaries as per the eligibility criteria of the scheme guidelines and 
selection/scrutiny of beneficiary lists are done by the States/UTs. The 
Scheme Guidelines and Unified Web Portal for submitting the online 
applications can be accessed through https://pmay -urban.gov.in. Based on 
the demand survey and selection of beneficiaries, the project proposals are 
prepared and approved by the State Level Sanctioning and Monitoring 
Committee (SLSMC) headed by the Chief Secretary of States/UTs for further 
consideration of release of Central Assistance by the Central Sanctioning and 
Monitoring Committee (CSMC).  However, the Government of Jharkhand 
decided to implement PMAY -U 2.0 only on 06.05.2026. No project proposal 
from Government of Jharkhand including Dumka is pending with the Ministry.

UDAN HELICOPTER SCHEME IN ODISHA  
175.    SMT SANGEETA  KUMARI SINGH DEO          
Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION 
be pleased to state:- 
(a) the details of helicopter services sanctioned under the UDAN Helicopter 
Scheme in Odisha during the period from 2020-21 to 2025-26; 
(b) the criteria adopted for the selection of districts under the UDAN Helicopter 
Scheme; 
(c) whether the Government has examined the feasibility of introducing helicopter 
connectivity for Balangir and Subarnapur in view of their distance from major 
airports and healthcare facilities and if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) the measures taken by the Gover nment to strengthen emergency medical 
evacuation and disaster response through helicopter connectivity in western 
Odisha? 
ANSWER 
Minister of CIVIL AVIATION      (Shri Kinjarapu Rammohan Naidu) 
(a) to (d): A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
****** 
  

STATEMENT REFERRED TO IN REPLY TO PARTS (A) TO (D) IN RESPECT 
OF LOK SABHA STARRED QUESTION NO. 175 FOR ANSWER ON 
30.07.2026 REGARDING "UDAN HELICOPTER SCHEME IN ODISHA" 
ASKED BY SMT SANGEETA KUMARI SINGH DEO. 
 
(a) to (d):  Helicopter operations under  the UDAN Scheme were introduced from 
the 2nd round of bidding in 2017 to enhance regional air connectivity in Priority 
Areas, namely Jammu & Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, the North -
Eastern States, Andaman & Nicobar Islands, and Lakshadweep Islan ds. Under the 
UDAN 5.1 round of bidding in 2023, the eligibility criteria was revised to allow 
helicopter operations provided that at least one origin or destination is a heliport 
and one of the locations lies in a Priority Area. No airline submitted bids 
connecting the helipads in Odisha with locations that lie within the Priority Areas. 
 
The next phase of the UDAN Scheme, launched on 04.07.2026, expands helicopter 
connectivity by envisaging the development of 200 modern helipads in 
Aspirational Districts, including in the State of Odisha and Priority Area districts 
where no heliport or airport is operational or under development, which will 
facilitate improved access for passenger connectivity as well as support emergency 
medical evacuation, disaster res ponse and relief operations in remote and 
underserved areas.

NO. 176 SHRI RAJPALSINH MAHENDRASINH JADAV: 
SMT. BIJULI KALITA MEDHI: 
 
Will the Minister of HOUSING AND URBAN AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) the status of implementation of the Urban Challenge Fund including the 
framework for project selection, funding pattern and the progress 
achieved during the Financial Year 2025- 26, particularly in Dahod Lok 
Sabha Constituency of Gujarat; 
(b) whether any guidelines have been issued for selection of cities and 
projects under the Fund and if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the details of the sectors proposed to be covered under the Fund 
including redevelopment of cities, water and sanitation infrastructure 
and urban mobility, particularly in Dahod Lok Sabha Constituency of 
Gujarat; and 
(d) the details of the planned financial outlay including the contribution of 
the Centre, States and other stakeholders? 
 
ANSWER 
THE MINISTER OF HOUSING AND URBAN AFFAIRS 
(SHRI MANOHAR LAL) 
 
(a) to (d): A statement is laid on the Table of the House.  
 
 
 
 

STATEMENT REFERRED TO IN REPLY TO PART (a) to (d) OF STARRED 
QUESTION NO. 176 DUE FOR ANSWER IN LOK SABHA ON JULY 30, 2026 
REGARDING “IMPLEMENTATION OF URBAN CHALLENGE FUND” 
(a) to (d): The Urban Challenge Fund (UCF) scheme has been 
operationalized with the launch of Operational Guidelines for UCF on 15th 
April, 2026. So far, 33 projects have been approved/ accorded in- principle 
approval. The State- wise details are given in Annexure. No proposal has 
been received from Gujarat State for Dahod Lok Sabha Constituency.  
 
The UCF provides a total Central Assistance of ₹1 lakh crore over the 
Mission period. Under UCF, Central Assistance is limited to 25 per cent of 
the cost of bankable projects, with the stipulation that at least 50 per cent 
of the project cost shall be fina nced through market -based sources, 
including municipal bonds, bank loans and Public- Private Partnerships 
(PPPs). The remaining project cost is to be met by the concerned 
State/UT/ULB. 
 
All Cities are eligible to participate under UCF . Chapter 7 of the operational 
guidelines includes details regarding the Project Appraisal and Challenge 
Framework including mandatory eligibility requirements, overall project 
flow/ implementation framework,  and project evaluation process for 
appraisal and selection of projects. The list of admissible projects under 
UCF are given under chapter 5 of the operational guidelines. The scheme 
guidelines are in public domain and may be accessed at  
https://www.mohua.gov.in/static/uploads/2026/04/7950afb9b2d5cb773ba3d
6c64bde9726.pdf  
 
UCF supports the development and strengthening of urban infrastructure 
through implementation of transformative and impactful projects under 
three verticals namely ‘Cities as Growth Hubs’, ‘Creative Redevelopment of 
Cities’ and ‘Water and Sanitation’.

DELAY IN DISBURSEMENT OF FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE UNDER PMEGP 
 
*177.  SHRI SHREYAS M PATEL:  
 
Will the Minister of MICRO, SMALL AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES be pleased to state: 
 
(a) whether the Government is aware of delays in the sanction and disbursement of financial  
assistance under the Prime Minister's Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP) in various  
States, including Karnataka and if so, the details thereof; 
 
(b) the number of PMEGP applications   received, sanctioned, pending, rejected  and disbursed 
during the last five years, State-wise and year-wise; 
 
(c) the average time taken for processing applications, sanctioni ng projects,  releasing margin  
money subsidy and disbursing loans under PMEGP; 
 
(d) the major reasons for delays in sanction and disbursement of assistance under  PMEGP and 
the corrective measures taken by the Government to address these issues; and 
 
(e) whether the Government proposes to simplify the approval process, strengthen  coordination 
with banks, introduce timelines for disposal of applications and  ensure timely release of financial 
assistance to eligible beneficiaries and if so, the details thereof? 
 
ANSWER 
 
MINISTER OF MICRO, SMALL AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES 
(SHRI JITAN RAM MANJHI) 
 
(a) to (e): A statement is laid on the table of the House. 
  

STATEMENT REFERRED TO IN REPLY TO PARTS (a) TO (e) OF THE LOK SABHA 
STARRED QUESTION No. 177 FOR ANSWER ON 30.07.2026 
 
(a):  The time taken for sanction of loans and disbursement of Margin Money subsidy under 
PMEGP in various States, including Karnataka, depends upon fulfillment of application process 
with supporting documents, appraisal of project viability and credit decision by the financing banks, 
deposit of own contribution and completion of Entrepreneurship Development Programme (EDP) 
training by the prospective beneficiaries and submission of Margin Money subsidy claims by 
financing banks.  
 
(b):  State-wise and year -wise details of number of applications received, sanctioned, pending 
and rejected by Banks; and number of applications for which MM Subsidy has been disbursed 
during the last five years under PMEGP is given at Annexure I.   
 
(c):  The average time taken for processing PMEGP applications by Implementing Agencies, 
sanction of loan by Banks and release of Margin Money (MM)subsidy by KVIC during the last five 
years is 58, 70 and 84 days, respectively.  
 
(d) and (e):  The Government closely monitors  the implementation of the Prime Minister’s 
Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP), including time taken in sanction and disbursement 
of financial assistance in the form of MM subsidy across the country, including Karnataka.  
 
Corrective Measures undertak en by the Government to streamline the approval process, 
strengthen coordination with financing banks for loan sanction, expedite disposal of applications 
and timely release of MM subsidy under PMEGP include the following: 
 
i. Pending applications and MM subs idy claims are regularly monitored and reviewed by the 
Government and financing banks through Quarterly Bankers’ Meetings at State and Zonal 
level, State Level Monitoring Committee (SLMC) and District Level Monitoring Committee 
(DLMC) meetings. 
ii. To assist applicants in preparing project proposals, more than 1,000 model Detailed Project 
Reports (DPRs) covering various sectors have been made available on the PMEGP Portal. 
iii. To reduce entry barriers, educational qualification requirements are waived for projects in 
manufacturing sector up to Rs. 10 lakh and in service sector up to Rs. 5 lakh. 
iv. To expedite approvals for small projects, EDP training has been exempted for projects up to 
Rs. 2 lakh. 
v. To provide guidance, facilitate applications and offer real -time assistance to prospective 
entrepreneurs, PMEGP Helpdesks have been established at State level and awareness 
programmes and financial literacy camps are conducted in all States/UTs, including 
aspirational districts, underperforming areas and North-Eastern Region. 
vi. PMEGP Portal developed as an end-to-end digital platform is integrated with financing banks 
through Jan Samarth Portal, streamlining the approval process and with SMS alert to 
applicants at different stages and facilitation of Udyam Registration.

GOVERNMENT OF INDIA 
MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION 
LOK SABHA 
STARRED QUESTION NO. : 178 
 ( TO BE ANSWERED ON THE  30th July 2026 )  
RISING PRICES OF AVIATION TURBINE FUEL  
178.    SHRI JANARDAN MISHRA                     
             SHRI SATISH KUMAR GAUTAM                 
 
Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION 
be pleased to state:- 
(a) whether the Government has taken any steps to provide relief to the airlines in view 
of the rising prices of Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF) globally and if so, the details thereof; 
 
(b) the details of the projected financial implications of such measures on airport 
operators and other concerned stakeholders; and 
 
(c) the criteria or parameters adopted by the Government for determining the nature  
and extent of relief measures to be provided to domestic airlines? 
ANSWER 
Minister of CIVIL AVIATION      
 (Shri Kinjarapu Rammohan Naidu) 
(a) to (c): A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
****** 
  

STATEMENT REFERRED TO IN REPLY TO PARTS (A) TO ( C) IN 
RESPECT OF LOK SABHA STARRED QUESTION NO. 178 FOR REPLY 
ON 30.07.2026 REGARDING 'RISING PRICES OF AVIATION TURBINE 
FUEL' ASKED BY SHRI JANARDAN MISHRA AND SHRI SATISH 
KUMAR GAUTAM.   
 
(a) to (c): The Government in consultation with stakeholders has taken 
several measures to support the aviation sector and help keep air travel 
affordable, which include:  
 
(i) For domestic operations, ATF prices were capped at a maximum 
increase of 25% over the 1 March 2026 base price, effective from 1 April 
2026 for the months of April and May 2026, 
(ii) Partial deferment of airport landing and parking charges for domestic 
operations at major airports along with a 25% rebate in such charges at 
Airports Authority of India (AAI) airports, 
(iii) Approval of ECLGS 5.0 with a total corpus of Rs. 18,100 crore, 
including Rs. 5,000 crore earmarked for Indian airlines, to provide liquidity 
support, 
(iv) Reduction of Value Added Tax (VAT) on ATF at Delhi (from 25% to 
7%) and at Maharashtra (from 18% to 7%) for 6 months.  
 
Further, the Government has approved a one-time ATF Price Stabilisation 
Fund (PSF) Scheme with a budgetary support not exceeding Rs. 10,000 
crore as a contingency measure in response to the exceptional sur ge in 
international ATF prices arising from the West Asia crisis, with the 
objective of protecting domestic airlines and ensuring operational stability.

GOVERNMENT OF INDIA

LOK SABHA 
STARRED QUESTION NO. 18 
 ANSWERED ON 20/07/2026 
  
Comprehensive Implementation Report Card for NEP 2020 
 
 
*18. Dr. K Sudhakar: 
 
Will the Minister of EDUCATION be pleased to state: 
 
(a) whether the Government has published a comprehensive implementation report card for 
National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, if so, the details thereof; 
  
(b) the details of the total number of schools developed under PM SHRI in the country along 
with the number of schools that are fully operational as model NEP schools, particularly in 
Karnataka; and 
  
(c) the details of the funds released to Karnataka and specific progress particularly in 
Chikkaballapur district under PM  SHRI, Samagra Shiksha and National Initiative for 
Proficiency in Reading with Understanding and Numeracy (NIPUN) Bharat in 2024 -25 and 
2025-26? 
 
 
ANSWER 
 
MINISTER OF EDUCATION 
 
(SHRI DHARMENDRA PRADHAN) 
 
 
(a) to (c):  A statement is laid on the table of the House. 
 
 
 
 
 
***** 

 
 
STATEMENT REFERRED TO IN REPLY TO PART S (a) TO ( c) OF THE LOK 
SABHA STARRED QUESTION NO. 18 ANSWERED ON 20.07.2026 ASKED BY DR. 
K SUDHAKAR,  HON’BLE MEMBER OF PARLIAMENT  REGARDING 
“COMPREHENSIVE IMPLEMENTATION REPORT CARD FOR NEP 2020” 
 
 
(a):  Implementation of National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 is a continuous process. It 
provides different timelines as well as principles and methodology for its implementation. 
NEP 2020 envisages operationalisation of the entire policy during the decade 2030 –2040, 
following which another comprehensive review will be undertaken. 
 UDISE + provides information on the changes in the Educational Indicators.  As per 
UDISE+ 2025-26 data, the enrolment in the schools has gone up to 24.72 crores.  The Net

*182.   Shri Miteshbhai Rameshbhai Patel: 
 Shri Rahul Singh Lodhi: 
 
Will the Minister of AYUSH be pleased to state: 
(a) the steps taken by the Government for global promotion and recognition of AYUSH  
systems including Ayurveda, Yoga, Unani, Siddha and Homoeopathy; 
(b) the details of international collaborations, MoUs and exports of AYUSH products and  
services during 2025-26; and 
(c) the progress made so far in the integration of AYUSH with modern healthcare systems both 
domestically and internationally? 
 
ANSWER 
THE MINISTER OF STATE (IC) OF THE MINISTRY OF AYUSH 
(SH. PRATAPRAO JADHAV) 
 
(a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

2 
 
The Statement referred in reply to Lok Sabha Starred Question No. 182 for 31.07.2026 
 
(a) and (b) Ministry of Ayush is implementing the central sector scheme for Promotion of 
International Cooperation for Ayush including Ayurveda, Yoga, Unani, Siddha, and 
Homoeopathy. Under this scheme the Ministry provides support to Indian Ayush drug 
Manufacturers/ Ayush Service providers to give boost to the export of Ayush products and 
services; facilitates the International promotion, development and recognition of Ayush 
systems of medicine; foster interaction of stakeholders and market development of A yush at 
international level; promote academics and research through the establishment of Ayush 
Academic Chairs in foreign countries and holding training workshop/symposiums for 
promoting and strengthening awareness and interest about Ayush Systems of Medic ine at 
international level.  
 The details regarding the export of Ayush products and services and MoUs signed by 
Ministry of Ayush, Govt. of India during 2025 -26 with foreign countries for promoting 
traditional systems of medicine is enclosed at Annexure-I. 
 
(c) Ministry of Ayush has undertaken several initiatives to promote the integration of Ayush 
systems with the modern healthcare system in the country. These include: 
National Level: 
i) Establishment of Ayush Vertical under DGHS (2023): An Ayush Vertical has been 
established under the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) through collaboration 
between the Ministry of Ayush and the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare (MoH&FW). I t 
serves as a dedicated institutional mechanism for planning, monitoring and supervising Ayush 
public health programmes and provides technical support for integration of Ayush into 
healthcare services, public health programmes, medical education and capaci ty building. The 
Ayush Vertical has developed evidence-informed Standard Treatment Guidelines to facilitate 
clinical integration. STGs for six common musculoskeletal disorders (2024) and five common 
metabolic disorders (2025) have been published. National Master Trainer programmes have 
also been conducted in collaboration with the Central Health Education Bureau, followed by 
cascading training across States and Union Territories.  
ii) Government of India has adopted a strategy of Co -location of Ayush facilities at Primary 
Health Centres (PHCs), Community Health Centres (CHCs) and District Hospitals (DHs), thus 
enabling the choice to the patients for different systems of medicines un der a single window. 
The engagement of Ayush doctors/ paramedics and their training is being supported by the 
Ministry of Health & Family Welfare under National Health Mission (NHM), while the support 
for Ayush infrastructure, equipment/ furniture and medicines is being provided by the Ministry 
of Ayush under National Ayush Mission (NAM), as shared responsibilities. 6302 PHCs, 3191 
CHCs and 475 DHs have been co -located across the country as per the NHM -Medical 
Information System (MIS) database as on 31.12.2025. 
iii) Integrated Ayush Departments have been established at Vardhman Mahavir Medical 
College (VMMC) & Safdarjung Hospital (2022) and Lady Hardinge Medical College (2023), 
New Delhi. These departments provide preventive, promotive and therapeutic healthcare 
services, including Panchakarma. Ayush Research Councils are also providing extended Ayush 

3 
 
OPD services at VMMC & Safdarjung Hospital, Lady Hardinge Medical College and Dr. Ram 
Manohar Lohia Hospital, New Delhi.  
iv) Details of initiatives taken by the Research Councils and National Institutes under the 
Ministry of Ayush for integration of Ayush with the modern healthcare system are given as 
Annexure-II. 
v) Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS) for Ayush Healthcare Facilities (2024): IPHS for 
Ayushman Arogya Mandirs and Ayush hospitals have been developed to standardize 
infrastructure, human resources, medicines and quality of service delivery, thereby 
strengthening the integration of Ayush services within the public healthcare system.  
vi) Public Health Advisories: The Ministry has issued Ayush public health advisories on Heat 
Wave (2024) and Monkey Pox (2024) in coordination with the National Centre for Disease 
Control (NCDC), supporting the integration of Ayush in national public healt h preparedness 
and response.  
International level:  
Ministry of Ayush, in collaboration with the World Health Organization (WHO), has 
undertaken several initiatives to facilitate the integration of traditional medicine into modern 
healthcare systems at the international level. These include: 
i) Launch of the ICD-11 Traditional Medicine Module 2 by WHO in New Delhi on 10 January 
2024, enabling the inclusion of morbidity codes for Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani in the 
International Classification of Diseases (ICD -11), thereby facilitating standardiz ed 
documentation and reporting of traditional medicine in health information systems. 
ii) Agreement between the WHO and the Ministry of Ayush, Government of India for the 
Development of Traditional Medicine intervention categories and index for the International 
Classification of Health Interventions (ICHI) with a holistic approach and with a focus on TM 
system of Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani. 
iii) Publication by WHO of the Development of WHO Terminologies on Ayurveda, Unani and 
Siddha, providing globally harmonized terminology to support clinical practice, education, 
research and policy. 
iv) Publication by WHO of the Benchmark Documents for Training and Practice of Ayurveda 
and Unani (2022) to promote standardized education, training and quality -assured clinical 
practice in line with international standards. 
v) WHO Technical Report on Training in Yoga, jointly developed by WHO and the Ministry 
of Ayush, establishes international standards for yoga training, enhancing the quality, 
credibility, and global integration of yoga into healthcare. 
vi) Establishment of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre (GTMC) in Jamnagar, 
Gujarat, as a global knowledge hub to strengthen evidence generation, research, innovation and 
the integration of traditional medicine into national health systems. 
vii) Bilateral cooperation through Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) with various 
countries for collaboration in traditional medicine, covering areas such as education, research, 
regulation, quality assurance and integrative healthcare. 
viii) Promotion of international dialogue on integrative healthcare through global conferences, 
ministerial meetings and WHO -led initiatives, including the two WHO Global Summit on 
Traditional Medicine held in India in 2023 & 2025, which emphasized evidenc e-based 
integration of traditional medicine within universal health coverage and primary healthcare. 

4 
 
ix) Facilitation of academic collaboration through Ayush Chairs and institutional partnerships 
with foreign universities and research organizations, promoting education, research and clinical 
exchange in integrative medicine.

and District hospital, Dimapur, Nagaland. The Council has 
also taken initiative to link Homoeopathy along with 
mainstream healthcare set-up by undertaking various Public 
Health programmes such as the Integration of NP CDCS 
Programme for Homoeopathy, Swasthya Rakshan program 
(SRP), the Programme ‘Homoeopathy for Healthy teething', 
a component of ‘Homoeopathy for healthy child and 
Schedule Caste (SC) Component plan’. 
4. Central Council for 
Research in Siddha 
(CCRS) 
CCRS has taken initiatives for integrating Siddha practices 
with the modern healthcare system by encouraging scientific 
research and clinical trials to validate the efficacy and safety 
of Ayush treatments along with modern treatments. 
Integrated Siddha can cer OPD has been functioning at All 
India Institute of Ayurveda campus and Siddha cancer OPD 
at Safdarjung hospital aiding the Palliative care of cancer 
patients through Siddha system through Siddha Clinical 
Research Unit, Safdarjung, New Delhi under CCRS. CCRS 
has signed MoU with AIIMS Rishikesh for initiating 
collaborative research activities for Cancer Management, 
Reproductive & Childcare and Regenerative Medicine. 
5. Central Council for 
Research in Yoga & 
Naturopathy 
(CCRYN) 
CCRYN has been undertaking collaborative research with 
premier institutions such as AIIMS, NIMHANS, IITs, S -
VYASA and other academic institutions to generate 
scientific evidence on the efficacy of Yoga & Naturopathy 
for various health conditions. The resea rch findings 
contribute to the evidence base supporting the integration of 
Yoga into preventive, promotive and integrative healthcare. 

10 
 
The Council also supports Yoga services through its Central 
Research Institutes of Yoga & Naturopathy (CRIYNs) and 
collaborative centres. 
6. National Institute of 
Siddha (NIS) 
This Institute is providing treatment for various diseases 
under Siddha System of medicine with modern health care 
systems both domestically and internationally for diseases 
like Cancer, Eye problem, Renal failure. 
7. Morarji Desai 
National Institute of 
Yoga (MDNIY) 
MDNIY has been designated as WHO-Collaborating Centre 
for Traditional Medicine (Yoga) since 2013. 
MDNIY has established 04 Yoga Therapy Centers in the 
medical institutes for Yoga Therapy and Research. 
MDNIY is running 20 preventive Health Care Units of Yoga 
in CGHS wellness centers in Delhi NCR. 
8. National Institute of 
Homoeopathy 
(NIH) 
National Institute of Homoeopathy has taken the following 
steps to integrate Homoeopathic system of medicine with 
the mainstream healthcare system in the field of education, 
research and healthcare services: 
i. In the National Institute of Homoeopathy, 
Kolkata, specialist doctors from Modern 
Medicine (10 doctors from General Medicine, 
Radiology & Imaging, Dermatology, Dental, 
General Surgery, Gynae& Obs., Oncology, 
Anesthetist and ENT) are engaged to provide 
expert opinion on the disease diagnosis and 
specially to demonstrate amongst students. In 
case of emergency, they prescribe allopathic 
medicines.  
ii. Further, NIH, Kolkata provides Homoeopathic 
consultation every Tuesday at Centenary 
Hospital, Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port, Kolkata 
along with mainstream medicine. 
iii. Development of evidence -based treatment 
protocols and clinical practice guidelines 
integrating Ayush with modern medicine for 
priority disease conditions. 
iv. Digital integration through Ayush Grid, Tele -
Ayush services, electronic health records and 
interoperability with modern digital health 
platforms. 
v. National Institute of Homoeopathy gives health 
care services following its fundamental 
principles synergistically with modern medical 
facilities. The facilities of X -RAY, USG etc. is 

11 
 
available in NIH with specialist doctors from 
modern medicine. The modern laboratory 
investigations are being done in NIH by Hind 
Labs on PPP model. 
vi. Students/Interns of NIH attends the trainings at 
the following modern medical facility centres: 
⎯ Internship Training at Chittaranjan Seva 
Sadan Hospital in the subject of 
Gynaecology and Obstetrics. 
⎯ Internship Training at Beleghata ID & BG 
Hospital, in the subject of Community 
Medicine.  
BHMS Students gets exposed for post mortem procedures at 
R G Kar Medical College and Hospital in the subject of 
Forensic Medicine and Toxicology. 
9. National Institute of 
Naturopathy (NIN) 
Institute is promoting coordinated and patient -centric 
integrative care through initiatives such as Yoga -based 
cardiac rehabilitation services in collaboration with the 
Centre for Chronic Disease Control (CCDC), integrative 
maternity services including cou nselling and Yoga, and 
lifestyle-based clinical services incorporating Naturopathy 
and Yoga interventions alongside conventional medical 
assessment and diagnostic services. 
10. North Eastern 
Institute of 
Ayurveda & 
Homoeopathy 
(NEIAH) 
NEIAH, Shillong has integrated modern practices in 
physiotherapy, dentistry and dietary etc. in its hospital to 
provide a comprehensive health care for patients benefit. 
Moreover, laboratory and radiology procedures are 
routinely conducted to supplement the Ayurvedic diagnosis 
of patients. As part of compulsory rotatory internship 
programme, NEIAH collaborates with the Primary 
Healthcare Centres by sending interns to various hospitals 
and PHCs under the Government of Meghalaya. 
11. National Institute of 
Ayurveda (NIA) 
National Institute of Ayurveda (NIA), Jaipur is actively 
working on several integrative healthcare initiatives to 
promote the integration of Ayurveda with modern 
healthcare systems through evidence -based research and 
collaborative studies. Some of the majo r initiatives are as 
follows: 
Two research studies in the field of Shalakya Tantra 
(Ophthalmology) are currently underway to evaluate the 
comparative efficacy and safety of Ayurvedic treatment and 
conventional modern medical treatment in the management 
of Non -Proliferative Diabetic Ret inopathy (NPDR) and 

12 
 
Anterior Uveitis. These studies are being conducted in 
collaboration with Sawai Man Singh (SMS) Medical 
College, Jaipur. 
NIA is collaborating with the Tata Memorial Centre, 
Mumbai on a research study titled "Anti -Cancer Effect of 
AYUR-LC (A Novel Ayurvedic Herbo -Mineral 
Formulation) in Non-Small Cell Lung Carcinoma (NSCLC): 
An In Vivo Experimental Study." This collaborative 
research aims to generate scientific evidence for the 
integrative management of cancer and strengthen the 
evidence base and credibility of AYUSH -based 
interventions. 
12. Institute of 
Teaching and 
Research in 
Ayurveda (ITRA) 
Two Joint Ph.D. Degree program between Academy of 
Scientific and Innovative Research (AcSIR) -CSIR-National 
Institute for Interdisciplinary Science and Technology 
(CSIR-NIIST), Trivendrum  and Institute of Teaching and 
Research in Ayurveda (ITRA). 
13. All India Institute 
of Ayurveda (AIIA) 
i. All India Institute of Ayurveda (AIIA) has adopted 
integrative healthcare model by collaborating with leading 
medical institutions for patient care, research, and education. 
ii. AIIA has also established research collaborations with 
universities and research organizations across countries 
including the USA, UK, Germany, Japan, Brazil, Australia, 
Canada and others for joint research, student exchange, 
faculty exchange, and training programmes. 
iii. The All India Institute of Ayurveda has 200 bedded 
tertiary care hospital with functional ICU. 
iv. The hospital functions as a model integrative medicine 
hospital for Ayurveda, and also has modern medicine 
specialists in various clinical, para clinical departments.  
v. The institute has established integrated oncology, chest 
diseases, metabolic diseases, Lifestyle diseases, 
Rheumatology, Skin clinics. 
vi. The institute has established 44 specialty outpatient 
departments, through which integrated treatments are being 
given. 
vii. AIIA has established extension centers at strategically 
important locations across India, Like in the premises of 
Supreme courts of India, at Lal Bahaddur Shastri Academy 
of Administrative Training, Mussoorie, Statue of Unity at 
Kevadia, Gujarat, IIT Delhi, Supreme Court of India. 
viii. AIIA has established functional integrated cancer clinic 
and research center at AIIMS, Jajjhar, and Integrative 

13 
 
medicine at Safdarjung Hospital, VM Medical College, New 
Delhi.  
ix. The AIIA hospital is accredited with NABH, prioritizing 
quality care to the patients 
x. Daily on an average there are over 1500 patient’s footfall 
is being recorded consistently at affordable cost.

STARRED QUESTION NO. *183
TO BE ANSWERED ON THE 31TH JULY,2026
NEED FOR MODERN HEALTH SERVICES IN AHILYANAGAR
*183 SHRI BHAUSAHEB RAJARAM WAKCHAURE:
Will the MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state:
(a) whether it is a fact that lakhs of devotees from across the country and abroad visit the
Shirdi Parliamentary Constituency in the Ahilyanagar district of Maharashtra daily which
necessitates the need for modern health services in the area, if so, the details thereof;
(b) whether high-level health services and super-specialty medical facilities are not available in the said
area and citizens have to depend on cities like Mumbai, Pune or Aurangabad for the treatment of serious
diseases, if so, the details thereof;
(c) whether the Government proposes to establish an AIIMS or a high-level super specialty hospital and
medical college on the lines of AIIMS in the said area; and
(d) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor, along with the future plan of the
Government in this regard, if any?
ANSWER
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE
(SHRI JAGAT PRAKASH NADDA)
(a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House.

STATEMENTREFERRED TO IN REPLYTO LOK SABHA
STARRED QUESTION NO. 183* FOR 31TH JULY,2026
(a) to (d): ‘Public Health’ & ‘Hospitals’ are State subjects. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
provides technical and financial support to the States/UTs to strengthen the public healthcare system,
based on the proposals received in the form of Programme Implementation Plans (PIPs) under National
Health Mission (NHM). Approval is accorded to the proposals in the form of Record of Proceedings
(RoPs) as per norms & available resources.
Health Dynamics of India (HDI) is an annual publication, based on healthcare administrative data
reported by States/UTs. Details of availability of health infrastructure including Primary Health Centres
(PHCs), Sub-Health Centres (SHCs), Community Health Centres (CHCs), Sub Divisional Hospitals
(SDHs) and District Hospitals (DHs) and other health units across the country including Maharashtra,
district-wise, may be accessed through the HMIS portal under Publications at the following link of HDI
2023-24:
https://hmis.mohfw.gov.in
Through 1.86 lakh Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (AAMs), including 13,457 AAMs in Maharashtra and
369 AAMs in Ahilyanagar district, comprehensive primary healthcare is provided by strengthening
Sub-Health Centres (SHCs) and Primary Health Centres (PHCs). These AAMs are required to provide
preventive, promotive, rehabilitative and curative care for an expanded range of services encompassing
reproductive and child healthcare services, Non-communicable diseases, Communicable Diseases,
Elderly and Palliative Care, Mental Health Care, Oral Health, Eye and ENT care and basic emergency
care.
Pradhan Mantri Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission (PM-ABHIM) is a Centrally Sponsored
Scheme (CSS) with certain Central Sector (CS) components, which has been implemented to strengthen
India's public health system through reforms that integrate health service delivery, public health action
and health research, thereby enhancing the capacity of public health systems to effectively respond to
pandemics and other public health emergencies. Total amount of Rs. 1,195.14 crore has been allocated
under PM-ABHIM for the State of Maharashtra for FY 2021-22 to FY 2025-26. Approvals have been
accorded to the State for 36 Integrated District Public Health Laboratories (IPHLs) and 36 Critical Care
Hospital Blocks (CCBs), amounting to Rs. 1086.44 crore including 1 IPHL and 1 CCB in Ahilyanagar
district.
Under Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana (PMSSY), setting up of 22 All India Institutes of
Medical Sciences (AIIMS) has been approved including one AIIMS at Nagpur in Maharashtra, which is
functional. Further, for expansion and strengthening of tertiary healthcare facilities in Maharashtra,
under another component of PMSSY upgradation of six (06) Government Medical Colleges/ Institutes
have been approved by way of construction of Super Specialty Blocks (SSBs) on Centre-State cost

sharing basis: (i) Grant Medical College & Sir JJ Group of Hospitals, Mumbai (ii) Government Medical
College, Nagpur (iii) Govt. Medical College, Aurangabad (iv) Govt. Medical College, Latur (v) Govt.
Medical College, Akola and (vi) Shri Vasantrao Naik Govt. Medical College, Yavatmal.
Under Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) for ‘Establishment of new medical colleges attached with
existing district/referral hospitals’, out of 157 medical colleges approved, 02 medical colleges have been
approved in Gondia and Nandurbar district in Maharashtra and are functional.

STARRED QUESTION NO. *184
TO BE ANSWERED ON THE 31TH JULY,2026
EBOLA VIRUS OUTBREAK
*184 SHRI BENNY BEHANAN:
SHRI CHARANJIT SINGH CHANNI:
Will the MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state:
(a) the measures taken by the Government after the World Health Organization declared the Ebola Virus
outbreak a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC);
(b) the number of individuals screened for Ebola Virus at airports in India between May and July 2026,
State/UT-wise and airport-wise;
(c) the precautionary and preparedness measures taken by the Government to respond to any suspected
or confirmed Ebola Virus Disease cases in the country; and
(d) whether the Government restricted the entry of travellers from countries affected by the Ebola
outbreak into India, if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor?
ANSWER
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE
(SHRI JAGAT PRAKASH NADDA)
(a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House.

STATEMENTREFERRED TO IN REPLYTO LOK SABHA
STARRED QUESTION NO. 184* FOR 31TH JULY,2026
(a) to (d): Following the declaration of the Bundibugyo Ebola disease outbreak as a Public Health
Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) by World Health Organization (WHO) and Public Health
Emergency of Continental Security (PHECS) by the Africa Centre for Disease Control and Prevention
(Africa CDC), the Government strengthened surveillance and public health preparedness across the
country in accordance with the temporary recommendations of WHO.
These measures have been undertaken in close coordination with National Centre for Disease
Control, Indian Council for Medical Research, Directorate General Health Services, Ministry of Civil
Aviation, Ministry of Home Affairs, Ministry of External Affairs, Ministry of Ports, Shipping &
Waterways,Department of Biotechnology and other stakeholders.
Enhanced screening and surveillance measures have been instituted at International airports and
other Points of Entry. In addition, advisories and Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) covering
surveillance, screening, quarantine, clinical management, laboratory testing and infection prevention
practices, case reporting have been issued to all States and Union Territories to ensure a coordinated
preparedness and response. As on date no case of Ebola Disease has been reported in the country. The
precautionary and preparedness measures undertaken by the Government are at Annexure 1.
The Government as such has not imposed a blanket restriction on the entry of travellers from
Ebola-affected countries. However, as per SOP for public health preparedness and response to Ebola
disease issued by the Government, all international passengers arriving at Points of Entry are screened
for a history of travel to Ebola disease affected countries namely Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC),
Uganda and South Sudan during the preceding 21 days.
As per the Self Declaration Forms submitted by international passengers including through the
Air Suvidha 2.0 portal, a total of 10,974 passengers coming from the aforesaid countries have been
screened from 23rd May uptil 28th July, 2026. The State/UT-wise and airport-wise details number of
individuals screened for Ebola Virus are at Annexure 2 & 3 respectively.

ANNEXURE 1
Measures undertaken by the Government after the World Health Organization declared the Bundibugyo
Ebola disease outbreak a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC);
 Issued detailed Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) and operational guidelines covering
surveillance, reporting, Infection Prevention and Control, technical specifications for Personnel
Protective Equipment, laboratory diagnosis, sample transportation, quarantine, isolation and
discharge of cases.
 Identification and operational readiness of designated isolation facilities across States and UTs.
 Expanded laboratory diagnostic capacity through ICMR-NIV ,Pune and additional designated
Biosafety Level-3 laboratories across the country.
 Ensuring availability of Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) and other logistics for healthcare
workers throughout the country including Points of Entry.
 Conducted mock drills in designated hospitals across all States/UTs to assess preparedness.
 Capacity building of APHOs, Bureau of Immigration officials, State Surveillance Units across
all states and designated isolation hospitals.
 Deployment of additional Human Resources (doctors & paramedical personnel) at all major
international airports.
 Mandatory submission of Self Declaration Forms (SDFs) for all international passengers
including through Air Suvidha 2.0 portal.
 Enhanced thermal and symptomatic screening at international airports and seaports for arriving
international passengers.
 Strengthened risk communication through airport displays, social media, awareness videos,
in-flight announcements and the 24×7 national helplines (1075).
 Activation of the NCDC Public Health Emergency Operations Centre (PHEOC).
 Regular coordination meetings with concerned Ministries, States/UTs, APHO offices and
designated isolation hospitals to review preparedness.

TO BE ANSWERED ON THE 31TH JULY,2026
STRENGTHENING OF AYUSHMANAROGYAMANDIRS
*185 SMT. MALVIKA DEVI:
SHRI NALIN SOREN:
Will the MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state:
(a) the number of Ayushman Arogya Mandirs approved and operational across the country,
State/UT-wise, district-wise and parliamentary constituency-wise for Nabarangpur, Bastar and
Kanker;
(b) the details of funds allocated, released and utilised for establishment, upgradation and
functioning of Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, in the country during the last three years,
State-wise and district-wise including the said constituencies;
(c) whether the Government proposes to further strengthen Ayushman Arogya Mandirs by
ensuring and increasing the specialized medical services, essential drugs, modern medical
equipments, digital health services, human resources, particularly in aspirational districts,
rural, tribal-dominated areas and underserved regions of the country, particularly under the
special provisions of the Union Budget 2026-27; and
(d) if so, the details thereof including the proposed establishment of new AAMs,
augmentation of manpower, diagnostic equipments, telemedicine facilities, essential
medicines, digital health infrastructure and financial assistance for improving accessibility
and effectiveness of primary health services in the country, State/UT-wise?
ANSWER
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE
(SHRI JAGAT PRAKASH NADDA)
(a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House.

STATEMENTREFERRED TO IN REPLYTO LOK SABHA
STARRED QUESTION NO. 185* FOR 31TH JULY,2026
(a) to (d) As reported by States/Union Territories (UTs) on Ayushman Arogya Mandir (AAM)
portal, 1,86,298 AAMs have been operationalized across the country, as on 30.06.2026. State/
Union Territory-wise number of AAMs operationalized across the country is enclosed as
Annexure-I.
As informed by Government of Odisha, a total of 213 AAMs have been operationalised in
Nabarangpur parliamentary constituency. As informed by Government of Chhattisgarh, a total
of 682 AAMs and 645 AAMs have been operationalised in Bastar and Kanker parliamentary
constituency respectively.
The National Health Mission (NHM) provides support for improvement in health
infrastructure, human resources in health facilities, availability and accessibility to quality
healthcare across the country. Technical and financial support is provided to the States/Union
Territories to strengthen the public healthcare system, based on the proposals received in the
form of Programme Implementation Plans (PIPs) under NHM. Approval is accorded to the
proposals in the form of Record of Proceedings (RoPs) as per norms & available resources.
Details of State/Union Territory-wise Central Release & Expenditure under NHM including
AAMs for the FY 2023-24 to FY 2025-26 is attached at Annexure-II.
Under the Pradhan Mantri Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission (PM-ABHIM),
support is also provided for infrastructure development for 11,001 Building less-AAMs and
5,456 Urban AAMs etc. The Fifteenth Finance Commission (FC-XV) had recommended
grants through Local Governments for specific components of the health sectors. Under
FC-XV support was provided for 9,863 urban AAMs towards strengthening of primary health
care.
The AAMs are required to deliver 12 packages of primary health care services across urban,
rural, tribal dominated and aspirational district areas, encompassing Reproductive and Child
Care Services, Communicable Diseases, Non Communicable Diseases, Palliative Care and
Elderly Care, Care for Common Mental Disorders, Substance Use Disorders Management, Oral
Health, ENT Care and Basic Emergency Care.
To complement the expanded services, the essential list of drugs & diagnostics has been
expanded to make available 179 drugs & 63 diagnostics at Primary Health Centre
(PHC)-AAMs and 113 drugs & 14 diagnostics at Sub Health Centre (SHC)-AAMs in the
country.
Under NHM, financial assistance is provided for augmentation of human resources, including
Community Health Officer (CHO), Auxiliary Nurse Midwife (ANM) and Multipurpose worker
-Male along with ASHAs in the catchment area for SHC-AAM and Medical Officer, staff
nurses, pharmacist, Health Assistants and Lab technician for PHC-AAM.
Comprehensive Primary Health Care (CPHC) services at AAM are supported by a set of

interoperable digital portals for digital recording and reporting. In an effort to establish
seamless data flow and continuity of care, this Ministry has launched Swasth Bharat Portal - a
centralized digital platform that provides single-window access to multiple national health
programs, thereby reducing the burden of data reporting on healthcare providers and
prioritizing patient care.
Further, the medicine availability has been strengthened through Drugs and Vaccine
Distribution Management System (DVDMS) portal to enable end-to-end digital inventory
management, real-time stock monitoring, and streamlined supply chain oversight to minimise
stock-outs.
As per AAM portal, a total of 31,347 AAMs in tribal districts and 27,775 AAMs in aspirational
districts have also been operationalised across the country as on 30.6.2026.
The teleconsultation services, available at all operational AAMs across the country, enables
people to access the specialist services closer to their homes addressing concerns of physical
accessibility, shortage of service providers and to facilitate continuum of care.
A total of 1,546 Mobile Medical Units (MMUs) are supported under NHM to provide
outreach services in remote villages with difficult terrain which are underserved and
inaccessible. Under National Ambulance Service, Advanced Life Support (ALS), Basic Life
Support (BLS), Patient Transport Vehicle (PTV), Boat ambulances, Bike ambulances and
Emergency Response Vehicles are supported under NHM for transportation of patients across
the country.

GOVERNMENT OF INDIA
MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE
DEPARTMENTOF HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE
LOK SABHA
STARRED QUESTION NO. *186
TO BE ANSWERED ON THE 31TH JULY,2026
DEPLOYMENT OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN PUBLIC HEALTHCARE
*186 SHRI SHASHANK MANI:
SHRI ARUN GOVIL:
Will the MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state:
(a) whether the Government has formulated a comprehensive roadmap for deployment of
Artificial Intelligence (AI) in public healthcare institutions to improve disease detection, diagnostics,
clinical decision support and health service delivery in the country;
(b) if so, the steps taken by the Government for its implementation, including the Government
healthcare institutions where such tools are operational or under pilot implementation;
(c) the measures being taken to promote the adoption of AI-enabled healthcare solutions in Government
health facilities, particularly in rural and underserved regions of the country, Statewise;
(d) whether a regulatory framework has been put in place to ensure ethical, secure and
responsible use of AI in healthcare, including the protection of patient data and transparency in
AI-based decision-making, if so, the details thereof; and
(e) the manner in which AI is expected to strengthen accessibility, affordability and quality of healthcare
services across the country?
ANSWER
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE
(SHRI JAGAT PRAKASH NADDA)
(a) to (e) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House.

STATEMENTREFERRED TO IN REPLYTO LOK SABHA
STARRED QUESTION NO. 186* FOR 31TH JULY,2026
(a) to (e) Yes, the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has launched the ‘Strategy for AI in
Healthcare’ (SAHI) on 17th February 2026 during the India AI impact summit. SAHI is a national
guidance framework to enable the safe, ethical, evidence-based, responsible and inclusive adoption
of artificial intelligence across India’s healthcare system. SAHI has been developed after extensive
consultation with several major stakeholders of the healthcare ecosystem.
The Ministry of Health has designated All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) Delhi,
Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research (PGIMER) Chandigarh and All India
Institute of Medical Sciences Delhi (AIIMS) Rishikesh as ‘Centres of Excellence (CoE) for artificial
intelligence’. The key objective of AI initiative of ‘centre of excellence’ is to promote development
and use of AI-based solutions in health.
Several AI solutions have been developed. Some of these include the CIinical Decision Support
System (CDSS) on e-Sanjeevani platform to provide symptom based clinical diagnosis and thus to
assist doctors in providing faster and more accurate consultations; Media Disease Surveillance under
Integrated Disease Surveillance Program (IDSP) to enable early detection and monitoring of disease
outbreaks; a Diabetic Retinopathy (DR identification solution) to assist in the timely screening and
diagnosis of vision-threatening eye diseases; AI enabled tools for identifying hotspots for TB,
Leprosy, Malaria, other vector borne diseases etc. for targeted interventions across the country,
including rural & underserved regions; AI-enabled handheld X-rays for TB screening & early
diagnosis through community outreach activities; TB Mukt Bharat App, featuring the AI-powered
Khushi Chatbot that provides medication reminders, treatment guidance, adherence support,
follow-up assistance, and nutritional and psychosocial support for TB patients. These AI solutions
are operational in collaboration with central and state health institutions across the country.
Together, these solutions address multiple aspects of healthcare including disease detection,
diagnostics, clinical decision support and health service delivery. Diabetic Retinopathy identification
solution enables early disease detection and treatment, CDSS supports possible differential diagnosis,
and MDS facilitates early outbreak detection and prompt public health action, while a range of
solutions for detection of TB and other AI health applications support health service delivery.
Further, safeguards for data privacy, consent and AI accountability are ensured by compliance to
various policies and guidelines issued from time to time. These include: Ethical guidelines for
Application of Artificial Intelligence in Biomedical Research and Healthcare by ICMR which
ensures that AI is developed, validated, deployed, and monitored in a manner that protects patients,
promotes public trust, and supports responsible innovation; India AI Governance guidelines by
MeitY which provides for a framework for the safe, trusted, inclusive, and responsible development,
deployment, and use of AI; Strategy for AI in Healthcare, which provides for a framework to enable

the safe, ethical, evidence-based, responsible and inclusive adoption of AI across India’s healthcare
system; Information Technology Act 2000 which governs electronic transactions and digital
governance; and Information Security Policy for Healthcare by the Department of Health and Family
Welfare which provides for a comprehensive framework to protect healthcare information systems
and sensitive patient data from cyber threats.
In addition, the Health Technology Assessment India (HTAIn), an attached office of the
Department of Health Research (DHR), Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW), evaluates
emerging AI and Digital Health Technologies (DHTs) for their safety, clinical effectiveness, value,
and scalability. Technologies with proven clinical effectiveness undergo a comprehensive Health
Technology Assessment (HTA), generating evidence to support their cost-effective adoption and
deployment in the public healthcare system. Further, Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation
(CDSCO) also regulates use of AI in health as medical device software under the Drug & Cosmetic
Act of 1940 and Medical Device Rules 2017.
